facts.fact: A thesis statement is one sentence, usually placed at the end of the introduction, that states the main claim the whole essay will argue.
facts.hook: a student realizes her draft has three good paragraphs but no sentence saying what they add up to

facts.fact: A strong thesis makes a claim that a reasonable person could disagree with; a statement nobody would dispute, like a plain fact, gives an essay nothing to argue.
facts.hook: a writing club member's thesis turns out to be something everyone already agrees with

facts.fact: A thesis should be narrow enough to prove in the space available; a claim about all sports everywhere is too broad for a short essay.
facts.hook: a thesis about 'technology' has to be cut down to fit a two-page assignment

facts.fact: A thesis can preview the argument by naming its supporting points in the same order the body paragraphs will discuss them.
facts.hook: a student reorders her body paragraphs and notices her thesis now lists them in the wrong order

facts.fact: An outline lists the main points and their evidence before drafting, so a writer can spot a weak or missing point before spending time on full paragraphs.
facts.hook: an outline on a napkin at a grandparent's table shows one point has no evidence at all

facts.fact: In a three-point argument, each point usually gets its own body paragraph, which opens with a topic sentence linking that point back to the thesis.
facts.hook: a friend reads only the first sentence of each paragraph and still understands the argument

facts.fact: Each point in an outline needs evidence listed under it, such as a fact, an example, a statistic or a quotation; a point with no evidence is just an assertion.
facts.hook: a student has to find a real example to go under a point he only 'felt' was true

facts.fact: A traditional formal outline labels main points with Roman numerals such as I, II and III, and the details under each point with capital letters such as A and B.
facts.hook: a younger sibling asks why the outline's numbers look like the ones on a clock

facts.fact: The three points in an argument must be truly different reasons; if two points say the same thing in different words, the argument really has only two.
facts.hook: a peer reviewer notices points two and three are the same reason in disguise

facts.fact: Some writers order their points from weakest to strongest, so the argument builds and the reader finishes on the most convincing reason.
facts.hook: a student debates whether to lead with her best reason or save it for last

facts.fact: A first thesis is often called a working thesis because it can change; if the evidence points somewhere else, a careful writer revises the thesis instead of ignoring the evidence.
facts.hook: research for an essay proves the opposite of what a student set out to argue

facts.fact: Outlining first separates planning from sentence-writing, so a writer decides what to say before worrying about how to word it.
facts.hook: a student stuck staring at a blank page tries writing a bullet-point plan instead

facts.fact: A five-paragraph essay has an introduction, three body paragraphs and a conclusion.
facts.hook: a student counts his paragraphs and finds he has written seven

facts.fact: A persuasive essay's goal is to convince the reader to agree with a position or take an action, not just to give information about a topic.
facts.hook: a report about school lunches has to be rewritten to argue for a change

facts.fact: An introduction often opens with a hook, such as a question, a surprising fact or a short story, to catch the reader's interest before stating the thesis.
facts.hook: a writing club tries three different first sentences for the same essay

facts.fact: A conclusion restates the thesis in fresh words and sums up the main points, but it should not introduce a brand-new argument.
facts.hook: a student's best new idea shows up in the last paragraph, where it does not belong

facts.fact: Many persuasive essays end with a call to action, a sentence telling the reader exactly what they should do next.
facts.hook: an essay about a local park ends by asking readers to sign a petition

facts.fact: In his Rhetoric, the Greek philosopher Aristotle described three ways to persuade: ethos, the speaker's credibility; pathos, the audience's emotions; and logos, logic and evidence.
facts.hook: a grandparent recognizes the three Greek words in a student's essay notes

facts.fact: A persuasive essay is stronger when it states the best opposing argument fairly and then answers it; this answer is called a rebuttal.
facts.hook: a student is surprised that admitting the other side has a point makes her essay more convincing

facts.fact: An ad hominem argument attacks the person making a claim instead of the claim itself, and it weakens a persuasive essay rather than strengthening it.
facts.hook: a draft calls the other side 'lazy' and a teacher circles it

facts.fact: The bandwagon fallacy claims something must be right or good simply because many people believe it or do it.
facts.hook: an essay's main reason turns out to be 'everyone at school wants it'

facts.fact: Transition words such as first, however, furthermore and therefore link paragraphs and show the reader how one idea relates to the next.
facts.hook: a choppy essay reads smoothly after a few connecting words are added

facts.fact: Naming where a statistic came from, such as the organization that published it, lets readers check it and makes a persuasive essay more believable.
facts.hook: a reader asks 'says who?' about a number in the essay

facts.fact: The word essay comes from the French essai, meaning an attempt; Michel de Montaigne used it as the title of his book Essais, first published in 1580.
facts.hook: a student learns her assignment is named after the word for 'a try'

facts.fact: In American English, a comma or period that ends a quotation goes inside the closing quotation marks; British usage often places it outside.
facts.hook: a story swapped with a pen pal abroad has its punctuation marked differently

facts.fact: In written dialogue, a new paragraph begins each time a different character starts speaking, so readers can tell who is talking.
facts.hook: a friend gets lost in a story where two characters talk in one long paragraph

facts.fact: When a dialogue tag follows a spoken sentence, the sentence ends with a comma inside the quotation marks instead of a period, as in "I'm ready," she said.
facts.hook: a writing club member marks every period before 'she said' in a draft

facts.fact: If a quoted line is a question, the question mark goes inside the quotation marks and the tag after it starts with a lowercase letter, as in "Where are you?" he asked.
facts.hook: a student wonders why 'He asked' should not have a capital H

facts.fact: When a dialogue tag interrupts one spoken sentence, the second part of the quote begins with a lowercase letter because the sentence is continuing.
facts.hook: a line of dialogue split around 'Mom said' looks like two sentences in a draft

facts.fact: In American English, a quotation inside another quotation uses single quotation marks within the double ones.
facts.hook: a character repeats what her brother said, and the writer is not sure which marks to use

facts.fact: The climax is the turning point of a story, the moment of highest tension when the main conflict is decided one way or the other.
facts.hook: a writing group argues over which scene in a draft is actually the climax

facts.fact: Rising action is the series of complications that raise the stakes and build tension before the climax.
facts.hook: a story that jumps straight to the big moment feels flat to its readers

facts.fact: After the climax, the falling action and resolution show the consequences of what happened and tie up the story's loose ends.
facts.hook: a reader asks what happened to the lost dog after the story's big rescue

facts.fact: Freytag's pyramid, based on Gustav Freytag's 1863 book on drama, pictures a plot as rising to the climax at its peak and then falling.
facts.hook: a student sketches her story's events as a mountain on the back of a worksheet

facts.fact: Deus ex machina, Latin for god from the machine, names an ending where an unexpected outside force solves the problem; in ancient Greek theater, actors playing gods were lowered by crane.
facts.hook: a draft's hero is saved by a sudden rainstorm and readers feel cheated

facts.fact: The protagonist is a story's main character, and the antagonist is the character or force working against them; their conflict drives the plot toward the climax.
facts.hook: a writer realizes her story's antagonist is a snowstorm, not a person

facts.fact: Mental health includes a person's emotional, psychological and social well-being, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
facts.hook: a health class poster makes a student realize friendships count as part of mental health

facts.fact: Stress is the body's response to a demand or challenge, and short bursts of it can help a person focus, such as before a test or a race.
facts.hook: a student notices her nerves before a recital actually sharpen her attention

facts.fact: During the fight-or-flight response, the adrenal glands release adrenaline, which makes the heart beat faster and breathing speed up.
facts.hook: a boy's heart pounds before a class presentation even though nothing dangerous is happening

facts.fact: Cortisol is a hormone made by the adrenal glands that rises during stress; when stress lasts a long time, cortisol can stay high.
facts.hook: a doctor explains why weeks of worry left a student feeling run down

facts.fact: Psychologists often separate fear, a reaction to a threat happening now, from anxiety, worry about a threat that might happen in the future.
facts.hook: a student feels anxious for days about a tryout that has not happened yet

facts.fact: Feeling anxious sometimes is normal, but when anxiety is intense, lasts a long time and gets in the way of daily life, a doctor may diagnose an anxiety disorder, which is treatable.
facts.hook: a friend explains that her anxiety got better after she told a doctor about it

facts.fact: Coping means the ways a person handles stress or difficult feelings; healthy coping strategies include exercise, getting enough sleep and talking with someone trusted.
facts.hook: two friends compare what each does after a bad day

facts.fact: Avoiding everything that causes anxiety brings quick relief but often makes the anxiety stronger over time, because the person never learns the situation is manageable.
facts.hook: a student who keeps skipping class presentations finds each one feels scarier than the last

facts.fact: Slow breathing with long exhales can calm the body's stress response, which is why it is a common coping skill before a stressful moment.
facts.hook: a goalie breathes out slowly before a penalty shot

facts.fact: A boundary is a limit a person sets about what they are comfortable with, such as how others treat them, touch them or use their belongings.
facts.hook: a student tells a friend she does not want her phone read without asking

facts.fact: A healthy boundary is about what you will do, not about controlling someone else, such as saying you will leave a conversation if it turns into yelling.
facts.hook: a teen decides what she will do if a group chat keeps turning mean

facts.fact: Resilience is the ability to adapt and recover after difficult experiences, and psychologists say it is a set of skills that can be built, not a fixed trait.
facts.hook: a player who missed the winning shot comes back to practice the next day

facts.fact: On the Holmes and Rahe stress scale, published in 1967, both changing residence and changing schools are listed as life events that require readjustment.
facts.hook: a counselor tells a new student that feeling off after a move is expected

facts.fact: A 2018 study by Jeffrey Hall of the University of Kansas found it takes about 50 hours together to turn an acquaintance into a casual friend.
facts.hook: a new student realizes one lunch together has not yet made them friends

facts.fact: The same 2018 study estimated that becoming a close friend takes more than 200 hours spent together.
facts.hook: a teen misses her old best friend and understands why a new one cannot appear in a week

facts.fact: In a 1950 study of a student housing complex at MIT, Leon Festinger and colleagues found residents most often became friends with the people who lived closest to them.
facts.hook: a new kid on the block becomes friends with the neighbor across the hall first

facts.fact: Homesickness is the distress of being away from home and familiar people; it is common after a move and usually eases as a person settles in.
facts.hook: a student cries over a photo of her old street, then laughs at her new friend's joke the next week

facts.fact: In the United States, a permanent change of address filed with the Postal Service forwards First-Class Mail to the new address for 12 months.
facts.hook: a letter from an old friend still finds its way to the new house

facts.fact: Joining a club or team at a new school puts a student in regular contact with the same people who share an interest, which gives friendships time to grow.
facts.hook: a new student signs up for the chess club to have somewhere to go at lunch

facts.fact: When a student changes schools, the old school usually has to send records such as grades and transcripts to the new one.
facts.hook: a new student is placed in the wrong math class until her records arrive

facts.fact: Animal welfare groups often advise keeping a cat indoors for a few weeks after a move, because some cats try to find their way back to the old home.
facts.hook: a family's cat keeps slipping toward the door of the new house

facts.fact: Friendships usually fade without contact, so friends who move apart and stay close tend to keep in touch regularly through calls, messages or visits.
facts.hook: two friends set a weekly video call before the moving truck leaves

facts.fact: Labeling each moving box with the room it belongs in and its contents makes unpacking faster, because boxes can be carried straight to the right place.
facts.hook: a teen cannot find her bedsheets on the first night in the new house

facts.fact: Researchers have found that the kind of time spent together, such as joking and sharing news, builds friendship faster than time spent side by side without talking.
facts.hook: a new student sits next to the same classmate for weeks but only becomes friends after a long bus ride talk

facts.fact: A checkable claim can be tested against evidence and shown to be true or false, while an opinion expresses a belief, feeling or judgment that evidence cannot prove.
facts.hook: two siblings argue at dinner and realize one is stating a fact and the other a taste

facts.fact: A checkable claim can be false; 'The Eiffel Tower is in Berlin' is a wrong factual claim, not an opinion.
facts.hook: a friend insists a false statement is 'just my opinion'

facts.fact: Judgment words such as best, worst, beautiful, boring and should are often signs that a sentence expresses an opinion.
facts.hook: a student highlights every 'best' in a product review

facts.fact: A single sentence can mix both: in 'The new park, which cost two million dollars, is a waste,' the cost can be checked but 'a waste' is an opinion.
facts.hook: a letter to the local paper about a new skate park gets pulled apart at the dinner table

facts.fact: A claim can be checkable even if nobody has checked it yet; 'most students at our school walk to school' could be tested with a survey.
facts.hook: a class decides to count how students really get to school

facts.fact: An opinion supported with evidence is still an opinion, but it is a more convincing one than an opinion given with no reasons.
facts.hook: a student backs up her argument for a crosswalk with a count of near-misses

facts.fact: A primary source is a firsthand record from the time, such as a letter, photograph or official data, and it is often the best place to check a claim.
facts.hook: a student checks a claim about the town's founding in the old newspaper archive

facts.fact: Professional fact-checkers use lateral reading: instead of judging a website by its own pages, they open new tabs to see what other sources say about it.
facts.hook: a slick website about a miracle drink turns out to be run by the company selling it

facts.fact: A reverse image search can show where a photo appeared online before, which can reveal that an old picture is being passed off as new.
facts.hook: a 'breaking news' flood photo turns out to be from years earlier

facts.fact: Confirmation bias is the tendency to accept claims that fit what we already believe and to doubt claims that do not, without checking either.
facts.hook: a student shares a story about a rival team without checking it because it sounds right

facts.fact: PolitiFact, a US fact-checking website founded in 2007, rates claims on a scale it calls the Truth-O-Meter, from True to Pants on Fire.
facts.hook: a family looks up a claim from a TV ad and finds it rated

facts.fact: A claim that cannot be checked even in principle, such as a vague promise that something 'changes lives,' gives readers nothing to test.
facts.hook: a student notices an ad makes no claim that could ever be proven wrong

facts.fact: In a 1954 study, Princeton and Dartmouth students watched the same film of a rough 1951 football game, and each school's students counted more fouls by the other team.
facts.hook: two friends who support rival teams leave the same game with opposite stories

facts.fact: In a 1974 study by Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer, people who were asked how fast cars 'smashed' into each other gave higher speed estimates than people asked about cars that 'hit.'
facts.hook: the way a parent asks about a hallway collision changes how a student remembers it

facts.fact: Akira Kurosawa's 1950 film Rashomon tells one crime through four witnesses whose accounts contradict each other.
facts.hook: four family members describe the same broken vase in four different ways

facts.fact: The parable of the blind men and the elephant, from ancient India, describes people who each touch a different part of an elephant and describe it completely differently.
facts.hook: a club argues about a project because each member has seen only one part of it

facts.fact: In February 2015 a photo of a dress went viral because some people saw it as blue and black and others as white and gold; the real dress was blue and black.
facts.hook: a family splits in half over the color of the same photo

facts.fact: The Rubin vase, introduced by Danish psychologist Edgar Rubin in 1915, can be seen as either a vase or two faces, but not both at the same moment.
facts.hook: two friends at a community centre see different pictures in the same poster

facts.fact: In the Sally-Anne test, first used in 1985, children from about age four usually say a character will look where she left her marble, not where it was moved while she was away.
facts.hook: an older sibling realizes a little cousin does not yet know others can believe something false

facts.fact: Psychologist Lee Ross named the fundamental attribution error in 1977: the tendency to blame others' actions on their personality while underestimating their situation.
facts.hook: a student assumes a classmate is rude, then learns he had just gotten bad news

facts.fact: Historians still do not know who fired the first shot at Lexington in April 1775; British and colonial witnesses each said the other side fired first.
facts.hook: a history club reads two eyewitness accounts of the same morning that disagree

facts.fact: In traditional Chinese culture white is worn for mourning at funerals, while in many Western weddings the bride wears white.
facts.hook: a family gathering has an awkward moment over what color to wear

facts.fact: Naive realism is the belief that we see the world as it really is, so people who disagree with us must be uninformed or biased.
facts.hook: two cousins each think the other is being unreasonable about the same family story

facts.fact: Two people can agree on every fact about an event and still interpret it differently because they value different things, such as fairness versus loyalty.
facts.hook: an after-school club splits over whether a teammate who covered for a friend did right

facts.fact: Most vegetable seeds need water, oxygen and warmth to germinate, but not light; a few, such as lettuce, sprout better with light and are sown very shallowly.
facts.hook: lettuce seeds buried too deep in a community garden never come up

facts.fact: A common gardening rule of thumb is to plant a seed about two to three times as deep as the seed is wide.
facts.hook: a student compares a tiny carrot seed to a big bean seed before planting

facts.fact: Frost-tender crops such as tomatoes, peppers and squash are planted outdoors only after the last spring frost, because freezing temperatures kill them.
facts.hook: a surprise cold night threatens seedlings planted too early

facts.fact: Seedlings grown indoors are usually hardened off, set outside for a little longer each day, so they can adjust to sun and wind before planting.
facts.hook: seedlings moved straight from a windowsill to the garden wilt in the sun

facts.fact: Beans and peas host bacteria in small lumps on their roots, called nodules, that take nitrogen from the air and turn it into a form plants can use.
facts.hook: a gardener pulls up a bean plant and finds little bumps on its roots

facts.fact: Squash plants grow separate male and female flowers, and only a female flower, which has a tiny fruit at its base, can grow into a squash after being pollinated.
facts.hook: a squash plant covered in flowers produces no squash at all

facts.fact: In the Three Sisters method used by many Indigenous peoples of the Americas, corn supports climbing beans, and squash leaves shade the soil against weeds.
facts.hook: a community garden plot copies a planting plan that is centuries old

facts.fact: A tomato is botanically a fruit, but in 1893 the US Supreme Court ruled in Nix v. Hedden that it counted as a vegetable for import taxes.
facts.hook: an argument at a farmers' market stand over whether tomatoes are fruit

facts.fact: A layer of mulch, such as straw or wood chips, keeps soil moist, blocks weeds from sprouting and evens out soil temperature.
facts.hook: one garden bed with straw stays damp while the bare bed beside it cracks

facts.fact: Under average conditions small radishes are ready to harvest about three to four weeks after sowing, but cold weather can slow them to six or seven weeks.
facts.hook: an impatient gardener plants radishes to have something to pick soon

facts.fact: Rotating crops, so the same plant family is not grown in the same spot year after year, helps keep soil pests and diseases from building up.
facts.hook: tomatoes planted in the same corner every year start getting sick

facts.fact: Watering deeply and less often encourages roots to grow downward, while frequent light sprinkling keeps roots near the surface where soil dries fastest.
facts.hook: two plots watered differently react very differently to a hot week

facts.fact: A note's pitch depends on how fast the sound source vibrates: faster vibration makes a higher pitch, and slower vibration makes a lower one.
facts.hook: a beginner hears a string's note drop as she loosens the tuning peg

facts.fact: Pressing a string at its exact midpoint halves the length that vibrates, and the note rises by one octave.
facts.hook: a guitar student finds the note at the twelfth fret matches the open string, only higher

facts.fact: A standard modern piano has 88 keys: 52 white and 36 black.
facts.hook: a student counts the keys on her grandparent's piano to check

facts.fact: The A above middle C is tuned to 440 vibrations per second in most modern music, a standard the International Organization for Standardization first recommended in 1955.
facts.hook: a band tunes to the same note on a phone app before rehearsal

facts.fact: Johann Maelzel patented the mechanical metronome in 1815, and Beethoven was one of the first major composers to write metronome markings in his music.
facts.hook: a student's metronome ticks a tempo marked in an old piece of sheet music

facts.fact: Bartolomeo Cristofori built the first piano in Florence, Italy, by 1700, and its name comes from Italian words for soft and loud, because it could play both.
facts.hook: a music teacher asks why the instrument is not just called the 'forte'

facts.fact: The treble clef is also called the G clef because its curl circles the staff line for the note G.
facts.hook: a beginner finally remembers where G is by tracing the clef's swirl

facts.fact: Pressing a trumpet valve sends air through an extra loop of tubing, making the air column longer and the note lower.
facts.hook: a student in a community center band wonders how three valves make so many notes

facts.fact: Practicing in several shorter sessions spread over days usually builds a skill better than the same total time crammed into one long session.
facts.hook: a student who practices only the night before each lesson keeps making the same mistakes

facts.fact: Studies have found that a night of sleep after practicing a finger-movement sequence can improve performance the next day without any extra practice.
facts.hook: a tricky piano passage suddenly goes better the morning after a frustrating session

facts.fact: Research on expert performers has found that how someone practices, focusing on specific weak spots, matters more than simply playing a piece many times.
facts.hook: a student stops playing the whole song and works only on the four measures she keeps missing

facts.fact: Pressing guitar strings repeatedly makes the fingertips sore at first; with regular practice, the skin toughens into calluses and playing hurts less.
facts.hook: a new guitar student wants to quit after a week of sore fingertips

facts.fact: Muscle soreness after new or hard exercise usually peaks 24 to 72 hours later, not right away; this is called delayed onset muscle soreness.
facts.hook: a player feels fine after the first practice and can barely climb stairs two days later

facts.fact: Delayed muscle soreness is not caused by lactic acid, which returns to normal levels within about an hour after exercise.
facts.hook: a teammate blames 'lactic acid' for soreness that started a day later

facts.fact: In 2009 Washington became the first US state to pass a youth sports concussion law requiring an athlete with a suspected concussion to be removed from play.
facts.hook: a coach pulls a player from the game after a hard hit, even though the player says he feels fine

facts.fact: Psychologist Bruce Tuckman proposed in 1965 that groups go through stages called forming, storming, norming and performing.
facts.hook: a new team argues a lot in the first weeks of the season before it starts to click

facts.fact: In 1977 Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen added a fifth stage, adjourning, for when a group finishes its work and breaks up.
facts.hook: players feel strange at the end-of-season party knowing the team will not be the same next year

facts.fact: In 1913 Max Ringelmann reported that as more people pulled on a rope together, each person's average pull became smaller.
facts.hook: in tug-of-war at practice, a coach notices some players easing off

facts.fact: Sweat cools the body as it evaporates, so in humid weather, when sweat evaporates slowly, athletes cool down less well and overheat more easily.
facts.hook: a sticky summer game leaves players more drained than a hotter but drier one

facts.fact: Growth plates, areas of growing cartilage near the ends of children's bones, are weaker than the bone around them, which is why young athletes have limits on repetitive stress.
facts.hook: a young pitcher is told he has reached his pitch limit for the day

facts.fact: Little League Baseball sets daily pitch limits by age, from 50 pitches for players aged 7 and 8 to 105 for players aged 17 and 18.
facts.hook: a coach checks the pitch counter before letting a pitcher finish the inning

facts.fact: Muscles grow stronger during recovery after training, not during the workout itself, so rest days are part of getting better.
facts.hook: a player who trains hard every single day starts getting slower

facts.fact: Across many sports, home teams win more than half their games on average, an effect known as home advantage.
facts.hook: a team that keeps losing on the road wins three straight at home

facts.fact: A team's winning percentage is its number of wins divided by the number of games played.
facts.hook: a player works out whether a 6-4 team or a 7-5 team has the better record
